query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the key to forming and maintaining a stable, coherent protective oxide scale above 900 °C is the selective oxidation driven by the surface segregation of the reactive X element. When the alloy is in a single-phase state, the homogeneous microstructure promotes uniform segregation of X to the surface, enabling the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide (e.g., alumina when X = Al or silica when X = Si). Conversely, in multiphase alloys, heterogeneous distribution and additional phase boundaries lead to uneven oxidation, inducing stresses that result in oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in either a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy specimens to temperatures above 900 °C under controlled oxidative or corrosive atmospheres
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in an oxidative/corrosive environment; comparison between single-phase and multiphase microstructures
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of microstructural homogeneity governs oxygen diffusion and reactive element segregation. A single-phase structure minimizes grain-boundary and interphase stresses, favoring uniform oxide formation, while multiphase boundaries disrupt this process.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature exposure, the reactive X element preferentially migrates to the surface and oxidizes. In a single-phase alloy, this yields a continuous, coherent oxide layer that adheres well due to minimal internal stresses. In contrast, multiphase alloys exhibit non-uniform oxidation along phase boundaries, leading to stress accumulation, oxide cracking, and eventual spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Single-phase alloys will develop a stable, uniform, and adherent protective oxide layer with minimal cracking or spallation, whereas multiphase alloys will form heterogeneous oxide scales that are prone to cracking and spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The baseline behavior is represented by unstable oxide film growth (non-coherent, cracked, or spalled oxide scales) typically observed in multiphase high-entropy alloys or when reactive element surface segregation is insufficient.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys subjected to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; the mechanism is influenced by the underlying metallic solid-solution state (single-phase versus multiphase).
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of reactive element (X) segregation and the quantitative influence of interphase boundaries on oxide adhesion remain uncertain; further experimental characterization is needed to refine these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples: one processed to achieve a homogeneous single-phase solid-solution and another engineered to exhibit a multiphase microstructure. Expose both sets to temperatures above 900 °C under identical oxidative/corrosive conditions. Characterize the surface oxide layers using microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and adhesion/spallation tests after thermal cycling.
measurements: Oxide layer continuity and thickness (via scanning electron microscopy)
Phase and chemical composition of the oxide layer (via X-ray diffraction or EDS)
Adhesion strength and spallation behavior (via standardized thermal cycling and mechanical adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the single-phase alloy does not exhibit a significantly more uniform, adherent, and coherent protective oxide layer compared to the multiphase alloy under these high-temperature conditions, or if both exhibit similar oxide degradation characteristics, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
